title: A drunk colleague at the Christmas party
situation: You keep well clear. Will still unravels in public. Afterwards people know who was near him, who helped, and who vanished. People notice that you treated it as not your problem, and it quietly costs you.

options.text: Check in afterwards and help him limit the damage
Be glad you stayed out of it, and leave it there

title: Your manager asks: individual contributor or management?
situation: You chose management for the pay and the team under you. Leading people is a different job altogether: other people's moods, the team's numbers, endless coordination. It is nothing like the deep technical work you are good at, and for a while you are badly out of your depth.

options.text: Face the gap, learn to manage properly, and grow into a decent people manager
Fail to manage well and let your technical edge slip, losing both

title: An unpublished restructure, and a friend about to buy a flat
situation: Sienna does not buy. She tells her husband, who “anonymously” discusses it in an industry group chat. The story reaches HR.

options.text: Tell HR the truth about how the leak spread
Deny it was you

title: Another department’s major incident: do you volunteer?
situation: The payments clearing centre had a P0 incident last night: a ledger service, unrelated to Halcyon Tech, is posting rubbish. Platform Engineering owns it, and your Lynx Payments team is not in the firing line. The platform director tags every payments tech lead in the leadership channel: “If you know ledgers, get here.” If you go, you face a week of on-call into the small hours, and your membership

options.text: Volunteer for the incident team
Offer two hours of remote Q&A in the channel, but do not join on site
Stay quiet and stick to your own work

title: Pay-review percentages are out — dwell on the ranking?
situation: Somehow everyone's pay-review percentage has been shared around the team, or a colleague has turned the figures into a comparison table. Yours is in the middle, neither top nor bottom. Looking at the table feels a bit awkward.

options.text: Look once, put it away, and spend your energy getting better so your next review is stronger
Keep staring at the ranking, feel more aggrieved each time, and let it hit your mood and your work
Take the comparison table to your manager and demand an explanation of every difference

title: Forced ranking: scoring a colleague who is also a friend
situation: Ethan’s bonus is roughly halved. He blocks you for three months. Some people on the team call you tough.

options.text: Try to explain the constraints of the rating system
Accept that the friendship is over

title: Client makes an inappropriate joke at dinner
situation: You laugh along to keep the client sweet. To everyone watching, that is taking part. Chloe is finished with you and will not work with you if she can help it. It gets round the team that you have no line when a deal is on the table. Your manager hears, and starts to doubt your judgement. Whatever goodwill you gained with the client, you have lost as much inside the company.

options.text: Own it: apologise properly to Chloe and admit you were out of order
Brush it off as ‘just dinner banter’ and insist you did nothing wrong

title: Dismissed in a team meeting as "just engineering work"
situation: Afterwards you book fifteen minutes with your manager and show how the work maps to business metrics. They soften: “Next time, put the business value on page one.” You still sense the rest of the team thinks engineering work does not count. You need to decide whether to fight for the team's visibility.

options.text: Push to get your work into team OKRs or the quarterly highlights
Keep to your own patch and stop speaking for the team

title: A project you wanted going to someone else
situation: After some hesitation, your manager agrees you can spend 20% of your week on the new project, as long as the live work does not slip. Two weeks later the live project hits an integration blocker, and Owen also needs you at the new framework's review.

options.text: Prioritise the live project, pause the new work, and tell your manager
Carry both, working weekends to do it

title: Hosting an important client visit
situation: An important client's head of engineering is visiting next week. Facilities has left the final plan to you, since you own the technical side of the partnership and will run the demo. There are three options. (A) Use the standard BD budget, drinks within policy included, for a working dinner at a nearby business restaurant, where you stay for two hours. (B) A working lunch in the office café, then

options.text: A: Working dinner at a business restaurant, staying two hours
B: Working lunch in the office café, then an afternoon demo covering everything in one go
C: Fully remote demo, no in-person visit

title: A new colleague with no sense of privacy
situation: You answered reluctantly, and Lou then chatted about your private life in the kitchen. Now it is out, you are on the back foot and wish you had drawn the line at the start.

options.text: Talk to Lou: ask her not to pass it on, and set the line from now on
Call her out for gossiping, in the team channel or in front of people

title: Stuck on the ladder: move into management or go deeper?
situation: You forced the move for the promotion. You neither enjoy nor are good at leading people, coordinating work or handling people problems. The team's results are flat, and the job never feels right. Having taken the role only for the grade, you find every day hard going.

options.text: Either put the work into becoming a capable manager, or admit it doesn't suit you and go back to the technical track
Grit your teeth in a role that doesn't suit you, and grow more bitter in it

title: A manager-free channel shares a screenshot of your boss
situation: You joined the mockery aimed at Chris himself, and the thread, with the screenshot and the jokes, was forwarded into channels that have nothing to do with the complaint. IT traces the chain. Handing the screenshot to HR, a representative, a union or a solicitor for the complaint is not part of what is being looked at.

options.text: Own up that you joined in
Deny it

title: An intern accidentally emails a rant about the manager
situation: Chris is silent for ten minutes, then says it must not happen again. Quinn gets a warning and keeps the internship.

options.text: Help Quinn write a proper wash-up
Step back and stay out

title: Going for a valuable certification that takes months
situation: There is a well-regarded certification in the industry that would help your career, but preparing for it would take months of evenings and weekends. The exam fee is not cheap either. You are not sure whether to start now.

options.text: Set a steady revision plan over several months, broken into daily tasks you can finish
Sign up, then study in fits and starts, and cram at the last minute
Drop the idea because it looks too hard

title: Where personal use of work kit stops
situation: Compliance confirm the current use sits inside 'limited personal use', and advise you to 'significantly reduce weekend usage to avoid perception issues'. The written confirmation is reassuring, and it also means the use is now on a formal record.

options.text: Cut weekend use as advised, and move most of the development onto personal kit in your own time
Keep using it, but avoid commit times colleagues can see, and stay quiet about it

title: A senior puts their name on an intern’s work
situation: Rowan turns on you in the room. Your manager tells you to “sort it afterwards.” Quinn’s name is added. Rowan freezes you out.

options.text: Walk your manager through the facts and ask for a fair rating
Take on some of Rowan’s work to thaw the relationship

title: You notice a remote colleague is often offline
situation: Your manager reviews the remote-working data, spots the unusual away time, and asks whether you knew.

options.text: Say you had noticed they were stretched, and suggest the manager speak to them directly
Say you did not know, and offer nothing further

title: Your idea is pitched first by someone else
situation: Now the team knows the history. People start calling it 'your idea'. The colleague is offended and says in a meeting they understand you had thought in a similar direction, but they developed their proposal independently and took it to delivery.

options.text: Publicly recognise their independent development and delivery, and make clear you never questioned that
Leave it. Let the team decide who contributed what

title: A toxic team culture: stay or leave?
situation: A newly hired VP is pushing an aggressive 'high-performance' culture: public humiliation for anyone who misses their numbers, briefings that reward stitching colleagues up, and a quiet rank-and-yank. The mood in engineering sours fast, and several people are showing signs of depression. One colleague privately asks you to go to HR together. Another tells you not to stick your neck out, because VPs

options.text: Join a few senior colleagues in a named letter to HR and the CEO about the culture
Keep your head down, and quietly help people who are being hurt to transfer internally

title: Training a model on customer conversations: where is the line?
situation: Product wants a 'smarter support' project: train a large model on old customer-service transcripts. It is technically feasible and could cut human support costs by about 30%. You find that the current privacy notice does not describe this use. Legal says you can sail close to the wind: ship first and update the terms later. That advice is a red flag. A notice does not by itself give permission to

options.text: Pause all use of the transcripts until the privacy lead has assessed whether it is allowed, and ship only if so
Train an MVP on public datasets, and run the compliance work in parallel

title: Late-night work messages and the manager's reaction
situation: Chris says, "In principle that's fine, but we can't slip client deadlines."

options.text: Set up an on-call rota, with no replies on days you are not on call
Keep to your hours anyway, whatever the reaction

title: A promotion without a pay rise
situation: You refuse in a huff and leave a sharp remark behind. Your manager does not force the issue, but marks you down as emotional and unwilling to step up. The title might have been a stepping stone, and a flash of temper has left you little room to manoeuvre.

options.text: Cool down and go back, spelling out the terms on which you would accept
Make the refusal final, with no way back

title: A colleague hogging the printer
situation: You need a short meeting pack printed now. Quentin is using the shared printer for a hundred-odd pages of personal material, checking each page as it comes out, with no sign of letting anyone in. You are short of time.

options.text: Explain politely that you have something urgent and ask to jump in for two pages
Walk over, cancel his job and print yours first
Wait in silence while the meeting starts without you

title: A drunk colleague at the Christmas party
situation: You stay for the show. Will fully unravels in front of your manager, becomes office comedy the next day, and gets a formal conversation about it. He later finds out you were right there watching and did not pull him back, and he is gutted. You have lost someone who could have become a friend.

options.text: Apologise to Will, and put in a fair word for him with your manager
Shrug it off — you didn’t pour the drinks

title: Pitching against a cheaper rival
situation: The company is bidding for a major client project, and you are leading the pitch. Your main rival is known for undercutting on price. The panel is a mix of technical people and procurement, so they care about both the solution and the quote. You have heard the rival will almost certainly lead with “we’re cheaper.” How you open will set the tone.

options.text: Play to your strengths: use technical depth and total cost of ownership to justify the higher price
Slash the price at the last minute to match them, and skate through the actual pitch
Take a swipe at the rival: imply their tech is weak and they have botched jobs before

title: Your first reaction to finding out a newer hire is paid more
situation: You find out by accident that a newly hired colleague in the same role, with less experience, is paid more than you. It rankles. What is your first move?

options.text: Collect yourself, gather your results, and ask your manager for a pay review at the right moment
Start coasting in protest and stop doing the work properly
Complain round the team about how unfair the company is, and spread the discontent

title: A junior asks to pair on your state machine
situation: Intern Alex asks for two hours this afternoon to pair, so he can understand a state machine you wrote. You have a bug that needs to be fixed by four.

options.text: Reschedule: pair first, then fix the bug
Point him at the docs and comments and let him work through it
Pair for an hour and do the rest asynchronously

title: Emergency hotfix — do you skip the process?
situation: The hotfix goes out in time and the live event carries on. When the process is completed afterwards, it finds an edge case the fix missed. The rollback is ready, so there is no second incident. The CTO asks you privately what would have happened if the rollback had failed.

options.text: Admit the risk, and propose a pre-authorised emergency path that sets out when the process can be shortened
Stress that this success shows the team's skill with incidents, and argue for keeping the current flexibility

title: Your manager hints that, after this long, you ought to be leading people
situation: Your manager needles you, half in jest: 'You're pretty senior on the engineering side — shouldn't you be thinking about leading people, moving up a bit? Staying on the tools forever isn't a plan.' Behind the joke, your manager clearly expects you to make the move soon. How do you answer the hint?

options.text: Take it as well meant, say whether you'd rather stay technical or try leading, and discuss a plan
Let one remark push you into agreeing to lead people, against what you actually want
Take it as a sign they are writing you off, and snap back

title: Should you put serious time into an emerging technology?
situation: An emerging technology is gathering pace in the industry and looks likely to become mainstream. Learning it properly would take a fair amount of your own time, and it will not help the work on your desk in the short run. Do you learn it, or leave it?

options.text: Treat it as an investment: make a plan, learn it properly, and look for chances to practise
Skip it as too much hassle and tell yourself you'll pick it up if you ever need it
Bookmark tutorials and sign up for a course so you look like you're learning, but never do the work

title: Abnormal health-check results: push through or see a doctor
situation: The company health-check results are in, and several of yours are flagged: abnormal liver function, a thyroid nodule recommended for further biopsy, and an ECG noting occasional extra beats. The doctor has written, 'See a specialist promptly; avoid late nights and high stress.' These two weeks are the quarterly delivery sprint, and your module is on the critical path. Going for follow-up tests mea

options.text: Take leave now for specialist tests and hand over your work cleanly
Push through this delivery and book the follow-up for the end of the month
Decide health checks always scare people, and ignore it

title: Communicating a breaking change on a public API
situation: The compatibility layer raises your maintenance cost, and your module's bug rate climbs.

options.text: Put a sunset date for the compatibility layer into the OKRs
Maintain it indefinitely

title: Raising a technical objection on another team's API design
situation: Both teams see your comment. Their owner replies: "Thanks for the data — there is a risk, but the timetable is tight. Let's ship as designed and watch it in a canary." Your manager also tags you: "Be careful how you raise things in public. They have a reputation to protect." You need to decide whether to keep pushing for a fix before go-live.

options.text: Insist on a pre-launch fix and attach a complete proposed patch
Accept the canary plan and add monitoring and a rollback playbook

title: A manager-free channel shares a screenshot of your boss
situation: In the Lynx late-night Slack channel, where no managers are allowed, someone posts a screenshot of Chris tearing into people: "If you can't even do this, what bonus do you think you deserve?" The next message: "Thoughts? Should we reply as a group?" You're in the channel. Passing a copy to HR, a staff representative, a union or a solicitor so they can deal with the complaint is not itself a discip

options.text: Ask them to stop spreading it, keep the evidence the target needs, and raise it through a grievance or staff rep
Join in and have a moan
Leave the channel and stay out of it
Message Chris privately about team morale, without saying how you know

title: In-house senior architect certification over the weekend
situation: The tech committee is running an in-house senior architect certification this Saturday and Sunday, on your own time. It is optional, and the company covers the fee. Meanwhile, an internal tooling project of yours is due next Tuesday as planned. If you put in extra hours this weekend, you could ship it on Monday morning, which your client contact says would save them a day of integration. You had a

options.text: Sign up for the certification and spend both days learning properly
Work through the weekend to deliver the project on Monday morning
Stick to the family weekend and pick work up next week as planned

title: Pitching against a cheaper rival
situation: You cut the price to almost nothing, and the pitch itself is thin. If you win, the team inherits a rushed, loss-making job. If you lose, you have still taught the client to expect a price you cannot live with. Your manager is uneasy about the tactic.

options.text: Stop cutting and steer the contest back onto value
Keep betting everything on price: win the deal now and worry later

title: Client makes an inappropriate joke at dinner
situation: You steer the conversation onto the project and give Chloe an easy exit — a ‘call she needs to take.’ The client does not clock that you defused it, and the table settles. Afterwards Chloe thanks you privately. You still have to decide whether the company should know this client has a problem with boundaries.

options.text: Brief your manager privately and factually, ask Chloe what support she wants, and raise it with the account lead
Decide it was handled and there is no need to raise it

title: Your idea is pitched first by someone else
situation: They say they do remember the chat, thought it was just thinking out loud, and had not realised how close it was to what they had in mind. They promise to credit you in later docs. The VP's impression of who proposed it will be hard to undo.

options.text: Accept the promise. Credit in the docs is enough
Ask them to say at the next update that the idea originally came from you

title: A dependent team is late — do you escalate in the open?
situation: A week later they still have not delivered, and your stopgap cannot fully cover the gap. In the project update your risk warning looks late. A VP asks why you are only saying so now.

options.text: Own your misjudgement of the risk, and ask for a more formal way of tracking cross-team dependencies
Point to the other team's history of slipping, and stress you could only judge what you could see

title: Colleagues want you to join a group pay demand
situation: A few colleagues unhappy with pay have organised and want to go to your manager together to 'push for an across-the-board increase'. They want you in: 'There's strength in numbers — come on.' You worry your manager will treat a group conversation as trouble. That would be his own reading. No rule says so.

options.text: Back a written case through a staff representative, and do not corner anyone
Decline the group pressure and make your own pay-review case on your contribution
Join in, and block the doorway so your manager cannot leave until you have an answer
Want to join but fear the blowback, so half-agree and then pull out at the last minute

title: A collaborator shifts the blame in a meeting
situation: You and Chloe air each other's failings in the meeting. The client frowns. Your manager cuts in: "Solve the problem first — don't bicker." Afterwards they speak to each of you separately.

options.text: Apologise to your manager and submit a plan for working together better
Insist Chloe shifted the blame first and ask your manager for a fair ruling

title: In-house kernel versus an open-source stack
situation: The platform goes live on the open-source stack on time and the business is pleased. Then a routine security scan flags a problem: this version has an undisclosed candidate CVE, and details are already circulating among a few people internally. If it can be triggered in production, it would hit your core clients. The call is yours.

options.text: Tell security and rush out a fallback from scratch
Sit on the report and bet it will not be triggered soon

title: An intern accidentally emails a rant about the manager
situation: IT shows the account was not hacked. You and Quinn are both investigated.

options.text: Admit you suggested the cover story
Blame Quinn

title: A chatty, skiving colleague eating into your time
situation: Luke, a teammate, has taken to hovering at your desk for half-hour chats: gossip, moaning, memes. You can tell their own workload is light and they mostly want someone to skive with. You have a critical module due for QA today and have already been interrupted three times. You need to decide how to handle it.

options.text: Tell them directly but politely that you need to focus today and to come back later
Put headphones on, look busy, and give them the cold shoulder
Chat for a few minutes, then steer back to work and mention today's deadline
Tell your manager that Luke keeps breaking your concentration

title: The client praises a feature you did not build
situation: The remaining payment comes in. Two months later the client finds there is no forecasting, and sends a solicitor’s letter alleging misrepresentation and asking for the money back.

options.text: Produce the review recording and the scope pack in your defence
Go along with sales and accept “poor communication” as the explanation

title: Your partner's job offer in another city: live apart, stay, or rethink
situation: You start living apart, kept together by weekends and video calls. The first months are fine. Then the travel wears you out, you miss important family moments, and the relationship and your energy both start to suffer. One night you race for a late train and turn up to a key review the next day in no fit state. You have to think again.

options.text: Agree a clear timetable for ending the distance, and plan your career around it
Keep putting off the decision and let things drift

title: The office war over windows and heating
situation: You made the call and the row stopped. Maya, who lost out, feels hard done by, thinks you sided with the majority, and is cooler with you afterwards. Shutting the argument down did nothing for the person in the minority.

options.text: Talk to Maya privately and find her a way to keep warm, to soften the blunt call
Majority rules. Nobody needs extra looking after

title: Company-wide AI tools, and the fear of being replaced
situation: You sink into anxiety, chasing rumours and refreshing Glassdoor. Your work visibly suffers. A more senior colleague says, 'Stop guessing when you'll be replaced and learn to use AI properly.' That pulls you back.

options.text: Put the anxiety to use: learn the tools and rebuild your edge
You know your colleague is right, but panic wins and you do nothing

title: Burnt out on the same work: reshape the job or not?
situation: You have been doing the same kind of work for a long time. You could do it with your eyes closed, and you cannot find any energy for it. You have stopped growing, the spark has gone, and deep burnout has set in. You can see that if this goes on, you will go stale. Do you reshape the job, or keep numbing your way through it?

options.text: Work out where the burnout comes from, and design a new direction or a reshaped role for yourself
Keep telling yourself a new job would fix it, and spend your energy on job boards and daydreams
Stay numb, coast, and stall your way through the days

title: A colleague who comes in ill
situation: You kept your distance and said nothing. Within a week three more people on the team are ill. In the review afterwards your manager says, 'If someone had said something, we could have sent her home.' You think back to keeping quiet, and regret it.

options.text: Learn from it and propose a simple team rule: if you're ill, stay off, and the team covers
Be glad you didn't catch it, and leave it there

title: A toxic team culture: stay or leave?
situation: You get two colleagues into healthier teams. The VP sees your 'little group' as a clique. In a one-to-one, they say they have heard you are helping people leave the team. If that is your attitude, you might as well join the department you have been sending people to, and free up the headcount for people who want to compete.

options.text: Take the 'suggestion' and transfer to the team you had already been helping people into
Refuse to be pushed into a transfer, and say you acted out of duty to your colleagues

title: Load-test results clash with what product expected
situation: You find the demo used an ideal path with an extremely high cache-hit rate.

options.text: Retest and issue a realistic capacity report
Compromise: ship, but with rate limits

title: Your company is acquired and the culture flips
situation: You learn the new rules, find the people who matter on the buyer’s side, and come across as open and capable, so they mark you down as someone they can rely on during the integration. They offer you a piece of cross-team work, which means acting as a bridge between two cultures. That is not easy.

options.text: Take the bridging role, get both sides working together, and build credibility with both companies
Duck the responsibility and push the cross-team work onto someone else

title: A chatty, skiving colleague eating into your time
situation: Luke pauses, says "fair enough", and leaves you alone that day. Over the next few days, though, they tell others at the tea point that "someone has gone rather chilly". You need to decide whether to repair the relationship.

options.text: Spend ten minutes with them at lunch explaining the boundary and that you mean no ill will
Offer no explanation and keep focusing on the work

title: Whether to volunteer as lunch-and-learn speaker
situation: The team's lunch-and-learn needs a speaker for the next slot. The topic is callback idempotency, which you have just worked on. Signing up means about 40 minutes of slides, and this week's calendar is already full.

options.text: Volunteer to speak
Suggest that Priya, who knows this area well, gives the talk
Don't sign up. Stay on delivery

title: You find out a peer got a bigger increase
situation: Pay-review outcomes are out. You learn privately that a peer at the same level got a larger increase. It sits badly, and you start to wonder whether you have been short-changed.

options.text: Compare contributions, find what you can improve, and if needed ask your manager how the assessment was done
Stew in jealousy, take against that colleague, and compete with them behind their back
Ask around what everyone got and spread the comparison to whoever will listen

title: A colleague who keeps handing you his work
situation: Dave on your team is very good at 'finding help'. One day it is two slides to rewrite, the next a script to run, and it is always 'you're better at this, it'll take minutes'. At first you were happy to help. Then you noticed more and more of his actual job coming your way as a matter of course, while he leaves early. Today there is another message: 'Mate, can you tidy this data? I've got to shoot

options.text: Help this time, and be clear: next time he drafts it first and you review
Decline gently: 'I'm swamped. You start it and I'll jump in if you're stuck'
Quietly take it on again so as not to sour the relationship

title: Your annual bonus falls short, and you go to your manager
situation: Your annual bonus comes in well below what you expected, after a year of graft and a rating that should have meant more. You are hurt and you have questions. Storm in, or get the facts first?

options.text: Check your rating, the bonus rules and last year’s figures, then book a conversation about how it was calculated
Storm into the office and demand to know why it is so low
Say nothing to their face, and snipe about the company in the team channel

title: After dinner, karaoke with someone on the promotion panel
situation: You put in an appearance and leave. Helen texts: “Sensible to get some rest.” Someone on the team mutters that you do not mix.

options.text: Bring breakfast in the next day for the people who stayed
Offer no explanation and let your work speak for itself

title: A colleague keeps @channel-ing questions already answered in the docs
situation: In the main project channel, new joiner Tessa @channels questions several times a day that are clearly in the docs or a thirty-second search away. Plenty of people are tired of the pings. This time it's a question answered on the first page of the wiki.

options.text: DM her a doc link and suggest checking the wiki or asking the owner before using @channel
Call Tessa out in the channel: "Could you read the docs before asking?"
Ignore it like everyone else and leave the question hanging

title: You notice a remote colleague is often offline
situation: They admit they are caring for family, and that they are already thinking about leaving. Their exit would leave a hole on a key project.

options.text: Help them ask your manager for flexible working, and try to keep them in the team
Tell them to decide in their own time, and stay out of it

title: An unpublished restructure, and a friend about to buy a flat
situation: You were copied on a restricted leadership note: a draft Q2 reorganisation. Lynx may be folded into Falcon Recs, with about 15% fewer roles. Nothing has been announced. Over dinner last night your friend and colleague Sienna said she wants to put in an offer on a flat, with the deposit already saved, and asked: “Is your team stable? I’m about to sign.” Her mother is ill and she needs the place.

options.text: Hint that things may move soon and she should be careful, without naming the document
Say you cannot comment on internal plans or promise that any role is safe, so she must weigh the risk herself
Tell her privately what is planned and ask her to keep it strictly confidential

title: Christmas-party rehearsals eating your evenings
situation: You stay late every night so you are not the weak link. Your actual work stacks up, and two month-end deliveries go wrong enough that your manager names you. A polished dance number does not make up for it. You can see you got the balance wrong.

options.text: Reorder your priorities: catch up on the work and put a limit on rehearsals
Keep putting rehearsals first and let the work wait

title: Lunch with the team, or keep the break to yourself
situation: After a month of lunching with the team twice a week, your manager stops talking about “mixing in”. Over lunch you learn Warren’s project is being folded into your module, so you have time to prepare.

options.text: Keep to the current pattern
Go to more lunches to stay more visible

title: You think the project bonus split is unfair
situation: A project closes and bonuses go out. You did most of the work, yet your share is roughly the same as people who barely showed up. The colleague who ran the split clearly favoured some over others. It feels unfair.

options.text: Raise your actual contribution with whoever ran the split or your manager, and ask for a fairer adjustment
Swallow it, say nothing, and go cold on the project from here
Lose your temper and threaten to coast on the next project, saying nobody should count on you

title: You overhear a redundancy list that includes a friend
situation: From a toilet cubicle you hear a VP and the HR director discussing the Q2 redundancy list: “…Ethan is in the consultation pool after the Lynx Wallet incident, package would be a standard redundancy…” Ethan is your tennis partner and helped you move last week. They wash their hands and leave, unaware you were there. The list has not been announced.

options.text: Tell no one and act as if you never heard it
Hint that Ethan should keep his head down and not resign in a hurry
Tell him he is on the list and what the package looks like
Tell Ethan only about the published redundancy process and support channels, and nothing you overheard

title: Should you take a transitional role mixing engineering and management?
situation: Your manager suggests a transitional role: managing two or three people while keeping part of your engineering work. It would let you test the move from individual contributor towards management with less at stake. It could also mean doing neither job well. Do you take it?

options.text: Take it as a low-risk trial of management, and plan how you will split your time
Play it safe, refuse any people responsibility, and stay a pure individual contributor
Take it but never split your time, try to do all of both jobs, and fail at both

title: Asking for remote work or a steadier role for family reasons
situation: Your family needs more of you. You are thinking of asking to work remotely or to move to a steadier, less intense role, but you worry it will look like a lack of ambition and hurt your promotion chances.

options.text: Be clear about the trade-off: make a formal request and commit to keeping your work up to standard
Make a vague request, because you want the easier setup but fear looking unambitious
Say nothing and keep grinding as you are

title: Balancing a promising idea against delivery pressure
situation: Three months of evenings produce a breakthrough and a solid case for the efficiency gain. When you ask your manager for formal resource, a colleague in the same sprint proposes a similar optimisation: it uses the current tech, ships sooner and gains less.

options.text: Compare the two on depth and long-term return, and argue yours is worth the bigger investment
Back the quicker option, and get your work put on the roadmap for later

title: Communicating a breaking change on a public API
situation: The reluctant team still stalls, then asks you for more time two weeks before the deadline.

options.text: Hold the deadline but offer a migration script and support
Slip another 30 days

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
situation: The team has one place at an industry conference. It is a good trip with plenty of visibility, and word is it will go to you or Jo. Your manager catches you in the kitchen and asks, as if in passing, 'How has Jo been lately? Do you think she's the right person to represent the team?' You can tell they are testing how you compete. The list is due next week.

options.text: Give Jo fair credit for her strengths and say she would be a good fit
Praise Jo, and briefly add your own recent relevant work
Say you each have strengths, and suggest choosing whoever fits the brief best
Hint at gaps in Jo's recent work

title: Dismissed in a team meeting as "just engineering work"
situation: You list SLA gains, a lower incident rate and fewer client complaints. Your manager pauses: “I have seen the data. Time is tight in the meeting. Next time, frame the update in business language.” Someone messages you afterwards: “Glad someone finally said it.” That afternoon your manager calls you in and hints that you should not steal the show in meetings. You need to decide how to carry on.

options.text: Reframe updates in business language, but keep the technical value in the write-up
Keep speaking up for engineering value in public and accept the political friction

title: Pushed on stage at the Christmas party
situation: You refuse bluntly. The host has to paper over an awkward few seconds. The people who were winding you up look silly, and your manager marks you down as “not really a team person.” There was a more graceful way to say no.

options.text: Recover by joining a later group game to show you are still part of things
Sit the rest of the night out with a face like thunder, speaking to nobody

title: A new manager is hired in, and you start again on trust
situation: A clear update and solid delivery make a good first impression, and they start taking your views seriously. Then they ask for something the last manager never would. People mutter in private that it is change for change’s sake.

options.text: Judge the new request on its merits, deliver it well, and add something useful
Join the private muttering that the old way was better

title: Client makes an inappropriate joke at dinner
situation: You are at a client dinner. After a few drinks, one of their senior people starts making jokes that cross a line — pointed, sexual remarks aimed at Chloe, a woman on your side of the table. Her laugh is tight and she looks trapped. They are an important account. Everyone else is pretending it is banter. The table is waiting to see what you do.

options.text: Change the subject without a scene, pull the talk back to the work, and give Chloe a way out
Join in and laugh along, to keep the ‘atmosphere’
Say firmly that the remark is not on, and bring the talk back to the work

title: A recruiter rings — do you take the call?
situation: A withheld number during work hours: a recruiter, wanting to talk about "a decent opportunity." You are not itching to leave, but it never hurts to know what the market looks like. How do you handle the call?

options.text: Arrange a time after work to hear them out, without disruption or commitment
Talk it through at your desk, loud enough that colleagues overhear
Hang up and block them, since even talking feels disloyal

title: You overhear an unpublished project naming you
situation: In the fifteenth-floor kitchen, platform director Harper and Miles, a fellow manager, drop their voices: “Polaris starts in Q3. On the Lynx side we’ll have… lead the tech.” The word you half-catch in the gap is your surname. The project has not been announced. If Miles realises you were listening, it may look like you were fishing.

options.text: Walk in as if you have just come for water and say hello as normal
Leave quietly and act as if you heard nothing
Stay in the corner and listen to the rest

title: A restrictive covenant on the way out: take the pay or keep your options
situation: You work through the clauses: scope, payment, and what happens if you breach. You also weigh the risk that your new employer would count as a competitor. Knowing all that, you can negotiate on equal terms: narrow the scope, raise the payment, or simply go somewhere the restriction does not reach.

options.text: Negotiate a narrower scope or a better payment, and sign a version both sides can live with
Choose a direction the restriction does not cover and avoid the dispute altogether

title: The pay-review pot is tight and you are competing for a rise
situation: You quietly make trouble for a rival. That kind of talk tends to travel. Managers dread someone who starts feuds and stabs colleagues in the back, and however capable that person is, they are hard to promote. You have staked your reputation as well as the rise.

options.text: Pull back before it goes further, stop the smearing, and compete on ability
Keep working against them behind their back

title: Abnormal health-check results: push through or see a doctor
situation: You deliver on time and the quarter looks excellent. At the end-of-month follow-up, the biopsy is another two weeks' wait. Meanwhile you get palpitations and fatigue, and your family starts pushing you to take it seriously. You can put it off again or stop the damage now.

options.text: Get treatment now, and tell the team you need some time to adjust
Keep putting off the follow-up as one project follows another

title: After dinner, karaoke with someone on the promotion panel
situation: You sing two songs. Helen says you are down to earth. At 1am she asks privately whether you are interested in Polaris — you cannot tell if it is drink talking.

options.text: Show interest and ask how to prepare for promotion
Talk about the project and leave promotion out, so it does not look transactional

title: Share options shrink in a buyback: living with the letdown
situation: You go through the option agreement line by line and find that some clauses of the buyback leave room to negotiate. With a few longer-serving colleagues you put a reasoned case. The company softens and offers a compromise: cash, a pay rise, or faster vesting. Now you choose: take something certain, or stay tied in.

options.text: Push for cash or a pay rise and turn paper value into real money
Trust the company's story again and accept a new option arrangement

title: An intern accidentally emails a rant about the manager
situation: Intern Quinn accidentally sends "Chris changes his mind like a rollercoaster" to the whole 200-person department. Two minutes later Quinn is in tears at your desk: "What do I do? I can't recall it." Chris is on the thread and has already read it.

options.text: Go with Quinn to apologise to Chris in person straight away
Suggest sending a follow-up claiming the account was hacked
Stay out of it and leave Quinn to deal with it
Call IT first and ask whether the email can still be recalled

title: Colleagues invite you on a self-funded conference trip
situation: You stay in the UK, follow the talks online and write notes. Someone teases that it does not count if you never left the house.

options.text: Turn the notes into a team session, and show that staying at home worked
Take the teasing to heart, stop writing notes, and give up on the online talks halfway

title: You survive a round of cuts and inherit the work
situation: You coast in protest at the overload, and the more that piles up, the more you half-do it. During a short-staffed, critical stretch you drop something. You survived the cuts, but because of how you have just performed, you are now a likely name for the next round.

options.text: Get your head straight, focus on the critical work, and steady your position
Keep coasting

title: A colleague who comes in ill
situation: Faye at the next desk has a heavy cold. She is coughing constantly and has almost lost her voice, but she is still in: 'The milestone's tight, I can't drop the ball.' The whole open-plan floor can hear every cough, and two people have started sneezing. She sees it as doing her duty, but there is a real risk she will pass it on. You are on the same project.

options.text: Check in privately, ask her to go home, and offer to cover the urgent part
Tell your manager her coming in ill is a health risk, and suggest sick leave while the team covers
Put on a mask, move away from the noise and the germs, and say nothing

title: A side project blurs the line with company business
situation: Compliance confirms you are not currently in breach, but suggests you sign an extra restrictive-covenant clause limiting how far you can take enterprise services later.

options.text: Accept the terms, so the side project stays within a legal framework
Challenge the extra clause as too broad, and propose a tighter definition of the boundary

title: A colleague's late handovers keep pushing back your work
situation: Your work cannot start until your colleague Will hands his over. He always delivers at the last minute. This time it arrives on the afternoon of the deadline, so you are stuck working late. He shrugs, "It was only a bit late."

options.text: Agree a handover time with him, and bring in the project schedule if it needs writing down
Work late to cover it and say nothing
Call him out in the main channel as always holding things up

title: A merge conflict wrecks release day
situation: Production hits an unexpected UI crash.

options.text: Roll back immediately and take responsibility
Make sure everyone knows whose feature it was

title: A new manager is hired in, and you start again on trust
situation: A new manager is hired in over your team, with a strong background and a style nothing like the last one. They do not know you yet. Some people are already sucking up to them; others are watching coldly. You start from nothing, and they will control your reviews and your prospects. What is your first move?

options.text: Lead with the work: explain clearly what you are doing and ask what they expect, without grovelling or bristling
Rush to pick their side and lay the flattery on
Watch them coldly, resist, and talk about how much better the last one was

title: Your manager asks: individual contributor or management?
situation: You avoided the decision and handed it to the company. You are parked in a role that suits neither your strengths nor your wishes. With no plan of your own, someone else has decided where your career goes.

options.text: Take the decision back, work out your direction, and tell your manager what you want
Keep drifting and see what happens

title: A collaborator shifts the blame in a meeting
situation: The client eases off, seeing you as someone who will own it. Afterwards Chloe says, "Cheers — lunch on me next time." Your manager privately reminds you to "watch how you communicate next time".

options.text: Fill your manager in on the facts so you do not become the permanent fall guy
Swallow it and do not pursue it

title: Share options shrink in a buyback: living with the letdown
situation: You take the loss as a warning, realise how long you have been tied to a future payday, and start testing your market value. A few conversations later it is clear you can get an offer with more guaranteed cash. Leaving in a rush also means giving up the relationships and the work you have built here.

options.text: Once you have an offer with more guaranteed cash, hand over cleanly and go
Take the outside offer to your company and negotiate better terms to stay

title: An undeclared relationship that looks like a conflict of interest
situation: Three months later that report is promoted. Other candidates feel the process was unfair and cannot say so. In an exit interview, one of them mentions 'an undeclared conflict in the promotion review'. HR traces it back and asks whether you knew.

options.text: Admit what you saw, and explain you were not sure at the time whether you should report it
Deny knowing anything. Insist you never saw anything unusual

title: Burnt out on the same work: reshape the job or not?
situation: You keep telling yourself a new place would fix it, and spend your energy on job boards and imagined exits. Then it dawns on you: you have not given yourself anything to grow into, and a new desk would bring the same repetition. The daydreaming has not eased the burnout, and the day job has suffered.

options.text: Stop treating the next job as an escape, and reshape your work and growth from where you are
Stay hooked on the fantasy that the next job will be better, while the current one keeps sliding

title: School run clashing with overtime
situation: Your child has just started school. Pick-ups and being there for your child both take time, and this project is busy. At this company, staying late has become the norm, and family time and work are clashing.

options.text: Share the load at home, agree some flexibility with the team, and make a formal flexible-working request for the school run
Throw yourself into the project and put family time on hold
Try to do everything perfectly at home and at work, and run yourself into the ground

title: Invited to shadow a senior planning meeting
situation: Your friend over-reads the hint, spreads anxiety through their team, and even starts looking for other jobs. The CTO hears that details of the meeting have leaked and starts tracing the source.

options.text: Go to the CTO, admit you shared no detail but may have hinted too strongly, and take responsibility
Deny passing anything on, and suggest their anxiety may have come from somewhere else

title: How thorough to be in code review as the team grows
situation: You leave more than thirty comments. The new colleague starts by working through them carefully, but after the third round they message you privately: should they run everything against your bar themselves before opening a PR? Your manager has noticed their PRs are merging more slowly and books a 1:1 to ask how you are reviewing.

options.text: Turn the standard into a team code-review checklist and roll it out
Go easier on this new colleague until they have found their feet

title: Annual bonus cut and paid in instalments
situation: The company announces that the annual bonus, which your contract describes as discretionary, is being reduced and paid over several quarters, citing 'cash-flow management'. A contractual sum could not be cut like this without your agreement. As it is, your expected pay takes a hit, and the move says something about how the business is doing.

options.text: Take it as a warning: look hard at the company's prospects and adjust your own plans
Complain in public and lead the moaning
Tell yourself at least they are still paying it, and try not to think about it
